co_never_winter_wall.blurb: A face-climbing wall in Staunton State Park, tucked above the Red Wall at roughly 9,000 feet. Seventeen routes, nearly all of them bolted: fifteen sport lines and a pair of trad climbs. Difficulty is concentrated in the low 5.10s, with a good handful of 5.7 to 5.9 routes for newer leaders and nothing much harder than 5.10. Expect just-off-vertical faces with bulges and overlaps rather than cracks, so bring soft shoes. The wall catches sun for most of the day, with a little morning shade, and it works well in cold months. The rock is fairly new, so wear a helmet. It takes a hike of a couple of miles to reach.

co_turtle_lake_cliffs.blurb: A sandstone cliff band just north of Durango, perched directly over the Turtle Lake boulders. It sees far fewer visitors than the bouldering below. Most of the seventeen routes are trad, with four bolted lines, and the styles run from face climbing to cracks. Grades cluster between 5.8 and 5.11, with a couple of routes harder than that, so it suits moderate and strong leaders but is thin for beginners. The stone is of varying quality, so choose lines carefully. Being close to town and right beside the road makes it an easy evening stop.
co_turtle_lake_cliffs.approach: A short trail leads past the boulders to the cliff band sitting directly above them.

co_cash_wall.blurb: A short, south-facing limestone wall in the Shelf Road area near Canon City, just northeast of the main Bank cliffs and across the road from Cactus Cliff. All seventeen routes are sport climbs. Grades start with one easy route in the 5.6 range and then build through the 5.9s and 5.10s into a solid group of 5.11 to 5.13 lines, so hard climbers have the most to chase while mid-grade climbers still get a few. The lines are fairly short, rock quality varies from line to line, and the sun hits it most of the day, making it a better choice in cooler weather. A trail runs along the base for easy walking between routes.

co_classy_cliff.blurb: One of three small crags in a roadside area below the Independence Pass gate, a few miles from Aspen. Routes are short, around 30 to 40 feet, and stacked close together, which makes it easy to hop between lines for a quick after-work session. Trad leads slightly in number over sport, and the spread runs from 5.8 up to low 5.12, with several 5.10s in the middle. It can be climbed through much of the year, winter days included. A steep little trail climbs from the parking pullout to the base.
co_classy_cliff.parking_note: Leave the car in the big pullout on the right side of the highway below the Independence Pass gate, roughly four miles from Aspen. Cross the road and step over the barrier to the trail.
co_classy_cliff.approach: A short but steep trail climbs from the road to the first crag, then splits at the top of it.
